title: Lesson 63: Prompt Management: Versioning, Testing, Prompt Libraries, and Prompt Ops
description: Inside the discipline around prompts: versioning them like code, holding them to a regression suite, sharing them through a findable catalog, and running prompt ops so a reworded prompt cannot regress silently.

questions.question: In the lesson's worked example, why does the support triage router use a semantic label like support-triage-router-v1.1.0 instead of just saving a new file?
options: Semantic versioning makes the file name shorter and easier to type in the terminal
It records the change history and lets the team roll back and identify which version runs in which environment
It is the only format the open-source eval tool accepts for test cases
It forces a full application redeploy on every prompt edit, which is the intended safety mechanism
questions.explanation: The lesson says versioning applies code-style tracking to prompts: a history of what changed and why, ability to roll back, and a record of which version runs in which environment. A semantic label like support-triage-router-v1.1.0 is that identity. It is about history and environments, not about OS compatibility or the eval tool.

questions.question: In the lesson's prompt regression workflow, what does the test suite do that a code commit message cannot?
options: It rewrites the prompt in a syntax the model parses faster
It verifies the prompt text is grammatically correct before deploy
It pins the behavior the queue depends on and blocks a change below a pass-rate threshold, catching regressions before users hit them
It signs the prompt with a cryptographic hash so no one can edit it
questions.explanation: The lesson describes a regression suite that pins the behavior a system depends on, for example routing a billing question to billing and an outage report to urgent, and blocks the deploy when the pass rate falls. Version history records that something changed; the eval suite is the gate that catches whether a change broke behavior before it reaches users.

questions.question: In the lesson's prompt ops layer, why does the team attach the prompt version to every production call and pair traces with evaluations?
options: To prove the prompt passes a spell check before it is published to the library
To increase token usage so cost reporting shows higher utilization
To make it impossible for another team to copy the prompt
So a quality drop becomes attributable: a trace-linked evaluation jumps from a flagged response to the exact prompt version, context, and model parameters that caused it
questions.explanation: The lesson's core prompt-ops habit is pairing trace and evaluation. Aggregate scoring says a problem exists; trace-linked evaluation supplies the why, because a 200-status LLM response can still be wrong, and the trace shows whether the drop correlates with a prompt version, model route, or retrieval source.
